content: The study included untreated patients diagnosed through clinical and laboratory microscopy using the Ziehl-Gabett method, treated patients diagnosed similarly, and healthy controls with no clinical or family history of the disease. The number of participants was 37 untreated, 36 treated (32 multibacillary and 4 paucibacillary), and 50 controls. The method of enrollment was not clearly described. Statistical techniques used included non-parametric tests for proportions, McNemar's test, chi-squared tests, and G-tests. The QUADAS-2 assessment for patient selection indicated a low risk of bias and low concerns regarding applicability. For index tests, the risk of bias was unclear, but concerns regarding applicability were low. The reference standard showed an unclear risk of bias but low concerns regarding applicability. Flow and timing were assessed with a low risk of bias. For paucibacillary (PB) cases, the sensitivity of the ND-O-LID test was higher than that of the PGL-I ELISA test. Both tests demonstrated high specificity and sensitivity. In endemic areas, the ML Flow test showed higher sensitivity (70%) compared to ELISA (53%), while specificity was similar for both tests at approximately 90%. The Duthie 2007 study evaluated MB and PB leprosy cases, household contacts, endemic and non-endemic controls, and tuberculosis (TB) patients. Diagnostic tests included ELISA, and outcomes measured were positivity rates. The study population included newly diagnosed MB and PB patients, healthy household contacts, and endemic controls with other skin conditions. Statistical techniques used included the Student's t-test. The Duthie 2014 study compared the Standard Diagnostics Leprosy test (SD) and ND-O-LID test using serum samples. Sensitivity and specificity were measured. The study population included newly diagnosed MB and PB patients, household contacts, and endemic controls. Statistical techniques included unpaired t-tests and ANOVA. The Hatta 2009 study assessed MB and PB leprosy cases, household contacts, healthy controls, and individuals with other conditions. Diagnostic tests included MMP-II (IgG) and PGL-I (IgM). Sensitivity and specificity were measured. Statistical techniques included ROC curve analysis and Student's t-tests. The Oo KN 2009 study evaluated MB and PB leprosy cases, household contacts, healthy controls, and TB patients. Diagnostic tests included ELISA-NTP-BSA and MMP-II. Positivity rates were measured. Statistical techniques included ROC curve analysis and Student's t-tests. The Prakash O 2006 study assessed MB and PB leprosy cases, healthy controls, TB patients, and individuals with other skin diseases. Diagnostic tests included 45-kDa PGL-I (ND-O-HAS). Positivity rates were measured. Statistical techniques included ROC curve analysis, chi-squared tests, and kappa values for agreement. The studies consistently demonstrated that seropositivity was higher in MB cases compared to PB cases. The ND-O-LID test showed higher sensitivity than PGL-I ELISA, particularly in PB cases. The ML Flow test was more sensitive than ELISA in endemic areas. The MMP-II test was more sensitive than PGL-I, especially in MB cases, but sensitivity was lower for PB cases. The RLEP qPCR test exhibited high sensitivity and specificity with a larger area under the curve (AUC). Blood samples were as effective as serum samples for the OnSite Leprosy Ab test.
